docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Here is the complete solution to run the 3-Hour Day 1 Workshop using a single content file.

To make this work with MkDocs, you strictly need two files: 1. mkdocs.yml (The settings file). 2. docs/index.md (The single file containing all your presentation slides, diagrams, and reference guides).

docs.title: 1. The Configuration File (mkdocs.yml)
docs.text:
Save this file in your main folder.

site_name: Linux for Biologists - Day 1
site_description: 3-Hour Intensive Foundation
theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    primary: teal
    accent: purple
  features:
    - navigation.sections
    - content.code.copy
    - toc.integrate

markdown_extensions:
  - admonition
  - pymdownx.details
  - pymdownx.superfences:
      custom_fences:
        - name: mermaid
          class: mermaid
          format: !!python/name:pymdownx.superfences.fence_code_format

docs.title: 2. The Single Content File (docs/index.md)
docs.text:
Save this inside a folder named docs. This file is divided into 4 logical sections to guide your 3-hour session.

# Linux & HPC: The Foundation (Day 1)

**Welcome to the 3-Hour Intensive Workshop for Biologists.**

!!! quote "Why use the Command Line?"
    "With the avant-garde technologies and constant evolution of scientific knowledge, biologists are faced with an increasing need for bioinformatics skills to deal with high-throughput data storage, retrieval, and analysis." 

    While GUIs exist, the command line is **faster**, **scalable**, and required for **cloud servers**.

---

## Part 1: The Architecture (Presentation)

### The "Onion" Structure
Linux is not just one program; it is a layered architecture.

```mermaid
graph TD
    User((User / Applications)) --> Shell[The Shell: CLI]
    Shell --> Kernel[The Kernel: The Brain]
    Kernel --> HW[Hardware: CPU, RAM, Disk]

    style Kernel fill:#f96,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style Shell fill:#61dafb,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
  1. The Kernel: The core of the OS. It manages hardware (RAM, CPU) and prevents conflicts between programs.
  2. The Shell: A program that exposes the OS to the user. It interprets your commands and forwards them to the kernel.
  3. The Terminal: The text-only window you are looking at right now.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Command
docs.text:
Commands follow a specific syntax. Let's dissect the command ls -l --sort time:

graph LR
    A[ls] -- "Command" --> Action(List Files)
    B[-l] -- "Option/Flag" --> Format(Long Format)
    C[--sort time] -- "Option with Value" --> Sort(Sort by Time)
    D[Documents/] -- "Argument" --> Target(Target Folder)

    style A fill:#f9f,stroke:#333
    style B fill:#ff9,stroke:#333
    style C fill:#ff9,stroke:#333
    style D fill:#9f9,stroke:#333
  • Command: The program you want to run.
  • Options (Flags): Switches starting with - or -- that change behavior.
  • Argument: The target (file or directory) the command operates on.

docs.title: Part 2: The Filesystem Tree (Visual Guide)
docs.text: In Linux, everything starts from the Root (/). It is an inverted tree structure.

docs.title: The Hierarchy Map
docs.text:
This structure is defined by the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS).

graph TD
    Root["/ (Root)"] --> Bin["/bin <br>(Binaries/Apps)"]
    Root --> Home["/home <br>(User Folders)"]
    Root --> Var["/var <br>(Logs/Data)"]
    Root --> Tmp["/tmp <br>(Temporary)"]

    Home --> User1["/home/ibdc"]
    Home --> User2["/home/rcb"]

    style Root fill:#ef5350,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style Home fill:#42a5f5,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px

docs.title: Key Directories
docs.text: Directory Description / The Root Directory (Start of the filesystem). /home Contains directories for users (e.g., /home/ibdc). /bin Essential command binaries (apps). /var Variable files like logs and databases. /tmp Temporary files (often deleted on reboot).

docs.title: 1. Where am I?
docs.text:
You are always in a "Current Working Directory."

$ pwd
/home/ibdc
  • pwd stands for Print Working Directory.
  • ~ represents your Home Directory.

docs.title: 2. Moving Around
docs.text:
Use cd (Change Directory). You can use two types of paths: * Absolute Path: Starts with /. (e.g., cd /home/ibdc/data) * Relative Path: Starts from where you are. (e.g., cd data)

!!! tip "Navigation Shortcuts" * cd ~ : Go Home. * cd .. : Go Up one level (Parent directory). * cd - : Go back to the previous directory.

docs.title: 3. File Manipulation (CRUD)
docs.text:
Essential commands for managing data.

  • List: ls -l (Long format), ls -lt (Sort by time).
  • Create: mkdir new_folder.
  • Copy: cp file1 copy1 or cp -r folder1/ folder_copy/.
  • Move/Rename: mv old.txt new.txt.

!!! danger "Warning: Deletion is Permanent" * rm file.txt: Deletes a file. * rm -r folder/: Deletes a folder and contents recursively. * There is no recycle bin in the command line.

docs.title: Part 4: Day 1 Reference (Future Guide)
docs.text: Save this section for your future work.

docs.title: Navigation & Files
docs.text: Command Action pwd Show current directory path ls -ltr List files sorted by time (reverse) cd .. Go up one directory cp -r Copy directory recursively mv Move or Rename rm -rf Force remove directory (Careful!)

docs.title: Viewing Content
docs.text: Command Action cat Display full file content less Scroll through file one screen at a time head -n 10 Show first 10 lines tail -f Follow file growth (live logs)

docs.title: Search & Wildcards
docs.text: Command Action * Wildcard: Matches zero or more characters (e.g., *.txt). find . -name "*.txt" Find all text files in current folder. grep "pattern" file Search for text inside a file.

docs.title: System Stats
docs.text: Command Action top Display running processes (CPU/RAM). du -sh Show directory size (Human readable). df -h Show total disk usage. ```

docs.title: How to use this:
docs.text:
1. Install: pip install mkdocs-material
  2. Create: Put mkdocs.yml in a folder. Create a subfolder docs and put the code above into docs/index.md.
  3. Run: Type mkdocs serve in your terminal.
  4. Present: Open your browser to http://127.0.0.1:8000. You will have a scrolling, interactive single-page site with all the visuals and tables ready for the biologists.

docs.title: Linux & HPC Workshop: Day 1 Foundation
docs.text: Welcome to the Linux & HPC Intensive. [cite_start]This single-page guide covers the architecture, filesystem, and navigation essentials required for modern bioinformatics[cite: 213, 236].

docs.title: Why Biologists Need the Command Line
docs.text: [cite_start]As high-throughput technologies evolve, biologists face an increasing need for bioinformatics skills to manage massive datasets[cite: 236]. * [cite_start]Efficiency: The Shell allows tasks to be done automatically and quickly[cite: 238]. * [cite_start]Reproduction: Proper commands allow you to repeat tasks exactly as many times as needed[cite: 239]. * [cite_start]Scale: Essential for interacting with High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems[cite: 333].

docs.title: Reducing Anxiety
docs.text:
• [cite_start]Mistakes are normal: Making errors is part of the process[cite: 403].
  • [cite_start]Safety: You cannot damage the hardware through normal commands[cite: 272].
  • [cite_start]Documentation: You are not expected to memorize everything; use this guide as a reference[cite: 330, 424].

docs.title: 2. Part 1: The Linux Architecture
docs.text:
[cite_start]Linux is a layered system where components interact to manage resources and execute programs[cite: 259, 260].

  1. [cite_start]Hardware Layer: The physical components (CPU, RAM, HDD)[cite: 270, 271].
  2. [cite_start]The Kernel: The "brain" that manages hardware and prevents program conflicts[cite: 246, 261, 262].
  3. [cite_start]The Shell: An interpreter that acts as a bridge, forwarding your requests to the kernel[cite: 267, 268].
  4. [cite_start]The Terminal: The interactive text window where you type commands and see results[cite: 279, 284].

docs.title: Anatomy of a Command
docs.text:
[cite_start]Every command follows a specific grammar: Command + Options + Arguments[cite: 312, 334].

[cite_start]ls -l --sort time Documents/ [cite: 314]

  • [cite_start]Command (ls): The action you want to perform[cite: 315].
  • [cite_start]Option/Flag (-l): Modifies behavior, such as switching to "long" format[cite: 316, 317].
  • [cite_start]Argument (Documents/): The object the command operates on[cite: 322, 323].

docs.title: 3. Part 2: The Filesystem Hierarchy
docs.text:
[cite_start]Linux organizes data in a hierarchical "Inverted Tree" called the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)[cite: 289, 346].

  • / (Root): The top-most directory. [cite_start]Everything starts here[cite: 292, 349, 350].
  • [cite_start]/home: Contains the personal directories for regular users[cite: 295, 348].
  • [cite_start]/bin: Important binary applications and commands[cite: 300].
  • [cite_start]/tmp: Temporary files that may be cleared upon reboot[cite: 300].

docs.title: 4. Part 3: Navigation & Operations
docs.text: Directories are like places. [cite_start]At any time, you are in exactly one place called your "Current Working Directory"[cite: 353].

docs.title: Essential Navigation
docs.text:
• [cite_start]pwd: Print Working Directory (Where am I?)[cite: 352, 355].
  • [cite_start]cd: Change Directory[cite: 370, 414].
    • [cite_start]cd ~: Teleport to your Home directory[cite: 378, 379].
    • [cite_start]cd ..: Move up one level in the tree[cite: 382].
    • [cite_start]cd -: Return to the previous folder[cite: 425].
  • [cite_start]ls -lhtr: List files in long format, human-readable, sorted by time (oldest first)[cite: 312, 425].

docs.title: File Manipulation
docs.text:
• [cite_start]mkdir <name>: Create a new folder[cite: 415, 425].
  • [cite_start]cp -r <src> <dest>: Copy a file or directory recursively[cite: 417, 425].
  • [cite_start]mv <src> <dest>: Move or rename a file[cite: 416, 425].
  • rm -rf <name>: Danger Zone. Forcefully and permanently remove data. [cite_start]There is no recycle bin[cite: 418, 419, 425].

docs.title: 5. Day 1 Command Reference
docs.text: Task Command Description Get Help man <tool> [cite_start]Open the manual; type q to quit[cite: 330, 331]. Search grep <pattern> [cite_start]Find specific text inside a file[cite: 425]. Inspect head / tail [cite_start]View the first or last 10 lines of a file[cite: 425]. Stop Ctrl + C [cite_start]Halt the current running command[cite: 425]. History Ctrl + R [cite_start]Search through your previous commands[cite: 425]. Find find . -name "*.txt" [cite_start]Search for files by name patterns[cite: 388, 389].

docs.title: Workshop Foundation: Linux & HPC for Biologists
Purpose of This Workshop
docs.text:
This workshop is designed to help biologists become confident users of Linux and High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments commonly used in modern biological research.

The goal is not to turn participants into system administrators or software developers, but to provide the practical understanding and confidence needed to work effectively on Linux systems and HPC platforms.

docs.title: What You Will Gain from This Workshop
docs.text:
By the end of this workshop, participants should be able to:

  • Understand what Linux and HPC systems are
  • Navigate files and directories on Linux systems
  • Follow and adapt command-line instructions
  • Run bioinformatics tools on servers or HPC
  • Submit, monitor, and manage jobs on IBDC-HPC
  • Use documentation to continue learning independently

docs.title: What This Workshop Is NOT
docs.text:
To reduce unnecessary stress, it is important to clarify that this workshop does not aim to teach:

  • Linux kernel development
  • Advanced system administration
  • Networking internals
  • Software engineering or programming concepts

These topics are outside the scope of this workshop.

docs.title: Why Biologists Need Linux and HPC
docs.text:
Modern biological research generates large and complex datasets, including:

  • Next-generation sequencing data
  • Mass spectrometry data
  • Imaging data
  • Multi-omics datasets

These datasets are often: - Too large for personal computers - Computationally intensive - Required to be processed in reproducible ways

Linux and HPC systems enable: - Efficient large-scale computation - Automation of analysis workflows - Reproducible and scalable research

docs.title: How Learning Will Happen in This Workshop
docs.text: This workshop follows a three-step learning approach:

docs.title: 1. Conceptual Understanding
docs.text: Participants first learn: - What the system does - Why certain tools and commands exist - How data and jobs move through the system

docs.title: 2. Guided Practical Sessions
docs.text: Participants then: - Follow step-by-step demonstrations - Type commands along with the instructor - Learn through small, controlled examples

docs.title: 3. Independent Revision and Practice
docs.text: After the workshop, participants can: - Revisit this documentation - Practice at their own pace - Apply concepts to their own research data

docs.title: A Simple Mental Model for Linux
docs.text:
Linux is not mysterious or complex when viewed correctly.

Think of Linux as a structured system that allows you to: - Store files - Organize data - Run programs - Automate repeated tasks

Key ideas: - Everything is organized into directories - Every file has a location - Commands are simple instructions to the system

docs.title: A Simple Mental Model for HPC
docs.text:
HPC systems can be understood using a simple analogy.

HPC is like a shared research facility: - Many users share powerful resources - You request resources instead of using them directly - Jobs wait in a queue - Results are produced later

Important concepts: - Login nodes are used for preparation - Compute nodes are used for execution - Job schedulers manage fairness and efficiency

docs.title: Reducing Fear and Anxiety
docs.text:
Participants should know that:

  • Making mistakes is a normal part of learning
  • Error messages provide useful information
  • Users cannot damage the system through normal commands
  • Asking questions is encouraged and welcomed

Learning Linux is a process, not a test.

docs.title: How to Use This Documentation
docs.text:
This documentation is intended to be:

  • A conceptual guide during the workshop
  • A reference for revision after the workshop
  • A support resource for future practice

Participants are not expected to memorize commands. Understanding concepts and workflows is the main objective.

docs.title: Workshop Ground Rules
docs.text:
• Type commands yourself during practice
  • Follow instructions step by step
  • Do not rush through exercises
  • Ask questions immediately if something is unclear
  • Support and help fellow participants

docs.title: What Success Looks Like
docs.text:
A participant has successfully completed the workshop if they can:

  • Log into a Linux or HPC system
  • Locate their data
  • Understand command-line instructions
  • Submit a computational job
  • Check job status and outputs
  • Know where to look for help

docs.title: Final Note
docs.text:
Linux and HPC are tools that empower biological research.

With the right foundation and guided practice, any biologist can learn to use them effectively.
